Title: Homes for Sale Near Me in Gastonia, NC | Ally Bohanan
Summary: How to set up a Gastonia home search that surfaces the right listings early, read between the lines of a listing and narrow down the right part of town.

Buying (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/buying/>) Gastonia, NCNo. 117

# Homes for Sale Near Me in Gastonia, NC: How to Search Smarter

How to set up a Gastonia home search that surfaces the right listings early, read between the lines of a listing and narrow down the right part of town.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 24, 20263 min read

In this article

- What should you do before you start searching?
- How do you choose the right part of Gastonia?
- How do you set up alerts that actually help?
- How do you read a listing like a pro?
- What should you check on a home you love?
- How do you tour efficiently?
- What do you get from living in Gastonia?
- New construction or resale?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

Get pre-approved first so you know your real price range. Then set instant alerts filtered by what matters most: commute, school assignment, lot size and home age. Learn what listing terms like "coming soon" and "under contract, due diligence" mean, and tour new listings quickly. A buyer's agent can flag homes that fit before you'd spot them.

## Key takeaways

- Search by commute and daily routine, not just ZIP code. Gastonia spreads out in every direction from I-85.
- Turn on instant alerts. Popular homes can draw several showings within the first few days.
- Check school assignment, flood status and HOA rules on any home you're serious about.
- Online home value estimates are rough. Use recent sold comparables to judge a price.
- Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves before you tour, so you can decide quickly.

Typing "homes for sale near me" into a search bar gives you hundreds of results and very little direction. If you're shopping in Gastonia (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/gastonia/>) , a bit of setup up front will save you weeks of scrolling and help you catch the right home before someone else does.

## What should you do before you start searching?

- Get pre-approved. Search within your real price range, not a guess. See our pre-approval guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mortgage-pre-approval-in-gastonia-nc-step-by-step-2026/>) .
- Know your monthly number. Include taxes, insurance and any HOA dues. Our mortgage calculator (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mortgage-calculator/>) helps.
- Write your must-haves and nice-to-haves. Bedrooms, garage, yard and office are often must-haves. A pool or finished bonus room is usually nice to have.

## How do you choose the right part of Gastonia?

Gastonia covers a lot of ground, and the right area depends on your daily routine. Try thinking in terms of what you want close by:

| If you want | Look at

| The fastest run toward Charlotte | Areas with quick access to I-85, plus the east side toward McAdenville (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mc-adenville/>) and Belmont (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/belmont/>)

| Trails and green space | The west side, toward Crowders Mountain State Park and Kings Mountain (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/kings-mountain/>)

| Older homes with character | Established neighborhoods near downtown

| Newer construction | Subdivisions toward the city's edges and along US-321 toward Dallas (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/dallas/>)

| Closeness to healthcare | Areas near CaroMont Regional Medical Center

Before you commit, test-drive the commute at rush hour and confirm the assigned schools for each address with Gaston County Schools.

## How do you set up alerts that actually help?

- Use a map boundary instead of a city name, so you don't miss homes with a different mailing address.
- Set your price range a little above and below your target. Some homes are priced to draw offers.
- Filter by your true must-haves only. Over-filtering hides good options.
- Turn on instant notifications. Daily email summaries are often too slow for popular homes.
- Ask your agent to set up an MLS search for you. It's usually the most current source available.

## How do you read a listing like a pro?

- Days on market: a long stay may mean room to negotiate, or a problem worth asking about.
- Price history: reductions and relists tell you how the seller's expectations have changed.
- Photo gaps: no photos of a bathroom or the backyard often means there's a reason.
- Status terms: "coming soon," "active," "under contract, due diligence" and "pending" each tell you something different about your chance to make an offer.
- Taxes and HOA: check the county tax record and the HOA dues before you get attached.

## What should you check on a home you love?

Before you write an offer, look into:

- Flood zone status (see our Gaston County flood zone checklist (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/flood-zones-in-gaston-county-nc-buyer-checklist-2026/>) )
- HOA rules on parking, fences, rentals and outbuildings
- Whether the home has city water and sewer, or a well and septic system
- Recent sold comparables, not online value estimates
- Planned road or development projects nearby, which you can find through the city or county planning department

## How do you tour efficiently?

Group showings by area, tour the newest listings first and take photos and notes as you go. Our guide to touring homes like a pro (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-tour-homes-like-a-pro-in-dallas-nc/>) has a printable checklist.

## What do you get from living in Gastonia?

Beyond the house itself, Gastonia gives you access to Crowders Mountain State Park, Rankin Lake Park, the Schiele Museum and an easy drive into Charlotte. Weekend ideas are in a weekend exploring Gaston County (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/lifestyle/a-weekend-exploring-gaston-county/>) .

## New construction or resale?

If you aren't finding what you want among the existing homes, building may be worth considering. Our buy or build guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/should-i-buy-or-build/>) compares both options. Ally also runs Bohanan Construction (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/bohanan-construction/>) , which builds custom homes in Gastonia.

When you're ready to see homes, Talk With a Buyer's Agent and we'll set up a search tailored to you.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why do some homes disappear from search sites so quickly?

Some go under contract fast. Others show as "pending" or "under contract" on one site and stay active on another because the sites update at different speeds. Your agent's MLS access gives you the most current status.

### What does "under contract, due diligence" mean in North Carolina?

It means the seller has accepted an offer, but the buyer can still terminate during the due diligence period. Some agents will accept backup offers on these homes.

### Should I look at homes that need work?

If your budget and timeline allow it, yes. Homes that need updating sometimes have fewer competing buyers. Get contractor estimates during due diligence so you know the true cost.

### Is it better to buy in Gastonia or a nearby town?

It depends on your priorities. Belmont, Mount Holly, Dallas and Kings Mountain each offer a different mix of price, commute and character, and our community comparison pages lay out the differences.

# Relocation Checklist for Families Moving to Gastonia, NC

A step-by-step relocation checklist for families moving to Gastonia: what to do before house hunting, under contract, moving week and your first month.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 22, 2026Updated November 16, 20262 min read

In this article

- What should you do before you start house hunting?
- What should you do while house hunting?
- What should you do once you're under contract?
- Which documents should you gather?
- What should you do during moving week?
- What should you do in your first month?
- Where can you learn more?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

Families moving to Gastonia should start with a budget and pre-approval, then confirm school assignment and commute for each home they consider. Once under contract, schedule inspections, utilities and school enrollment. After the move, update your driver's license, vehicle registration and voter registration with North Carolina, and find doctors, parks and activities nearby.

## Key takeaways

- Work the move in phases: planning, house hunting, under contract, moving week and first month.
- Confirm school assignment with Gaston County Schools by address before you make an offer.
- Gather school records, immunization records and proof of residence early.
- Utility providers can differ by address, including inside and outside Gastonia city limits.
- New North Carolina residents need to update their driver's license and vehicle registration with NCDMV.

Moving a family means juggling homes, schools, jobs and a hundred small tasks at once. A checklist keeps the important things from slipping. Here's a phased plan for families relocating to Gastonia, from the first budget conversation to your first month in town.

## What should you do before you start house hunting?

- Set a monthly payment you're comfortable with, then run scenarios with our mortgage calculator (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mortgage-calculator/>) .

- Get pre-approved. Start with our preferred lender (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/our-preferred-lender/>) .

- List your must-haves: bedrooms, yard, commute limits, school priorities.

- Research schools on Gaston County Schools (<https://www.gaston.k12.nc.us>) and the NC School Report Cards (<https://ncreports.ondpi.org>) .

- Compare Gastonia with nearby towns. See Gastonia vs. Kings Mountain (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/communities/compare/gastonia-vs-kings-mountain/>) and our communities page (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/communities/>) .

- Review local background on Census QuickFacts for Gaston County (<https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/gastoncountynorthcarolina>) .

## What should you do while house hunting?

- Confirm school assignment for each home with the district, not a listing or map app.

- Drive the commute at rush hour, and time trips to school, groceries and the doctor.

- Ask about HOA rules, fees and amenities.

- Check flood zones on the FEMA Flood Map Service Center (<https://msc.fema.gov>) .

- If you can't tour in person, ask your agent for live video tours and neighborhood drive-throughs.

## What should you do once you're under contract?

| Task | Notes

| Schedule inspections | Do it right away; your due diligence period is limited

| Get insurance quotes | Your lender will need proof of homeowners insurance

| Confirm closing logistics | North Carolina closings are handled by an attorney; ask about remote signing if needed

| Book movers | Get quotes early, especially in summer

| Set up utilities | Providers can differ by address; confirm electric, water, sewer, gas, trash and internet

| Contact schools | Ask about enrollment steps and required documents

## Which documents should you gather?

- Birth certificates and immunization records for each child.

- Recent report cards, transcripts and any IEP or 504 plans.

- Proof of residence (closing documents or lease).

- Medical and dental records, and prescriptions.

- Pet vaccination records.

- Vehicle titles and registration.

## What should you do during moving week?

- Do a final walkthrough before closing.

- Pack an essentials box: chargers, medications, bedding, school supplies, snacks.

- Confirm utilities are on in your name.

- Change the locks and garage codes after you move in.

- Locate the water shutoff and electrical panel.

## What should you do in your first month?

- Update your driver's license and vehicle registration through NCDMV (<https://www.ncdot.gov/dmv>) ; check its site for new-resident deadlines.

- Register to vote at your new address.

- Find a pediatrician, family doctor and dentist.

- Check your property tax listing with Gaston County.

- Explore parks, libraries, youth sports and activities. The Gaston Regional Chamber (<https://www.gastonchamber.com/>) is a good place to find local organizations.

# https://allybohananrealestate.com/how-to-negotiate-repairs-after-inspection-in-mcadenville-nc/

Title: How to Negotiate Repairs After Inspection in McAdenville, NC
Summary: How to sort inspection findings, decide between repairs and credits, and put agreements in writing before due diligence ends in McAdenville.

Buying (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/buying/>) McAdenville, NCNo. 115

# How to Negotiate Repairs After Inspection in McAdenville, NC

How to sort inspection findings, decide between repairs and credits, and put agreements in writing before due diligence ends in McAdenville.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 19, 2026Updated November 16, 20263 min read

In this article

- How does repair negotiation work in North Carolina?
- How should you read the inspection report?
- Which repairs are worth asking for?
- How do buyers and sellers negotiate well?
- When should you ask for a credit instead of a repair?
- How do you close smoothly after repair talks?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

After an inspection in McAdenville, sort findings into safety, major systems, and minor or cosmetic items, then ask only for what really matters. Support requests with photos and contractor estimates, consider credits or a price change when repairs are complex, and get every agreement in writing before your North Carolina due diligence period ends.

## Key takeaways

- In North Carolina, repair negotiations happen during the due diligence period, so start right away.
- Focus on safety, water, roofs and major systems, not cosmetic items.
- Contractor estimates make requests more credible than opinions.
- Credits give buyers control of the work but may be limited by loan rules.
- Put who does what, by when and how it's verified in writing.

The inspection report is where many deals get tense. A long list of findings can feel alarming to a buyer and insulting to a seller. In practice, most of it is routine, and a calm, organized approach usually gets both sides to closing.

McAdenville is a small town of about 650 people, known as Christmas Town USA, with many older homes alongside newer ones. That mix shapes what inspections tend to find.

## How does repair negotiation work in North Carolina?

Under the standard North Carolina offer to purchase, there's no separate repair contingency. Instead, the buyer has a due diligence period to inspect, investigate and negotiate. During that window, the buyer can usually terminate for any reason, though the due diligence fee generally goes to the seller.

That makes timing critical:

- Schedule inspections as soon as the contract is signed.

- Leave time for specialists if the general inspector flags something.

- Get contractor estimates for major items.

- Submit your request with enough time left for a response and counter.

- Sign a written agreement before due diligence ends.

Unless the seller agrees in writing, they generally aren't obligated to make repairs.

## How should you read the inspection report?

An inspection report records conditions on the day of the inspection. Many items are maintenance, not defects. Focus on:

- Structure: foundation, framing, roof

- Major systems: HVAC, plumbing, electrical

- Water: active leaks, crawl space moisture, grading and drainage

- Safety: outdated wiring, missing GFCI protection, smoke detectors, railings

In older homes, expect findings like aging components or older construction methods. Some are normal for the age of the house, and others need a specialist's opinion. Our guide to handling inspection surprises calmly (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-handle-inspection-surprises-calmly-in-cherryville-nc/>) helps you keep perspective.

## Which repairs are worth asking for?

| Priority | Examples | Typical approach

| High | Active leaks, roof damage, unsafe electrical, failing HVAC, structural concerns | Request repair, credit or price change

| Medium | Aging but working systems, minor drainage fixes | Consider a credit or note for future budgeting

| Low | Cosmetic wear, older but working fixtures, personal taste | Usually leave out of the request

Overreaching can cost goodwill and time. Buyers protect themselves best by focusing on protection, not perfection. Sellers do best by responding to the important items rather than refusing everything.

## How do buyers and sellers negotiate well?

For buyers:

- Group requests into major and minor items

- Attach photos, report excerpts and contractor estimates

- Offer solution options: a repair, a credit or a price adjustment

- Keep the tone respectful

For sellers:

- Respond to the high-priority items first

- Consider offering selected repairs or a credit instead of all or nothing

- Think about your timeline and what a relisting would cost you

- Remember that a future buyer's inspector would likely find the same issues

Market conditions matter. When buyers have plenty of choices, sellers are often more flexible. When competition is strong, buyers may limit requests to major defects.

## When should you ask for a credit instead of a repair?

Credits let buyers choose their own contractor and control the quality of the work, and they save sellers from managing a project. Consider a credit when:

- The repair needs a specialist

- You're concerned about workmanship

- The closing timeline is tight

- The issue doesn't affect financing

Loan programs can limit seller concessions or require certain repairs before closing, so check with your lender before you agree to a credit. Make sure the amount realistically covers the work.

If an inspection raises bigger construction questions, Ally's background helps. She also runs Bohanan Construction (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/bohanan-construction/>) , a custom home builder in Gastonia, and she reads inspection reports with a builder's eye.

## How do you close smoothly after repair talks?

Your written agreement should spell out:

- Exactly what will be repaired

- Who will do the work, and whether a licensed contractor is required

- The completion deadline

- How completion will be shown, such as receipts or a re-inspection

Then schedule the work early, confirm any lender requirements and check everything at the final walk-through. For more on staying on schedule, see how to avoid closing delays (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-avoid-closing-delays-in-lincolnton-nc/>) , and learn more about living in McAdenville (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mc-adenville/>) . Buying here? Talk With a Buyer's Agent and we'll walk through your inspection report with you.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the seller required to make repairs in North Carolina?

Generally no, unless they agree to in writing. Under the standard NC contract, the buyer's protection is the due diligence period, during which they can negotiate or terminate.

### What happens if we can't agree on repairs?

If you're still within due diligence, the buyer can usually terminate, though the due diligence fee generally goes to the seller. Talk with your agent about options before deadlines pass.

### Should I get a re-inspection after repairs?

It's a good idea for significant items. At minimum, ask for receipts and the contractor's description of the work, and check it at the final walk-through.

# https://allybohananrealestate.com/buying-waterfront-property-in-lake-wylie-sc/

Title: Buying Waterfront Property in Lake Wylie, SC | Ally Bohanan
Summary: A due diligence guide for South Carolina–side lake homes: access types, shoreline and depth, Duke Energy dock permits, flood insurance, taxes and financing.

Buying (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/buying/>) Lake Wylie, SCNo. 114

# Buying Waterfront Property in Lake Wylie, SC

A due diligence guide for South Carolina–side lake homes: access types, shoreline and depth, Duke Energy dock permits, flood insurance, taxes and financing.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 17, 20265 min read

In this article

- What kind of water access are you buying?
- How do you judge the shoreline and depth?
- What does Duke Energy control?
- How should you inspect the dock?
- What will insurance cost?
- How are property taxes different in South Carolina?
- Does the lake change through the year?
- How does financing work for waterfront homes?
- Waterfront buyer checklist
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

Buying on Lake Wylie means checking more than the house. Confirm the type of water access, the water depth at the dock, and that any dock is permitted by Duke Energy. Check the FEMA flood zone and get insurance quotes early. Then line up a lender who knows waterfront appraisals and, often, jumbo loans.

## Key takeaways

- "Lake property" can mean direct frontage, deeded access, a community dock or just a view; confirm which in the deed.
- Duke Energy manages Lake Wylie and permits docks and shoreline work, so verify any existing dock's permit.
- Ask about water depth at the dock when lake levels are lower, and inspect the dock separately from the house.
- Flood zone, flood insurance and higher homeowners premiums belong in your budget from the start.
- On the South Carolina side, owner-occupants can apply for the lower 4% legal residence assessment ratio on property taxes.

Lake Wylie is the waterfront market closest to Charlotte. It sits on the Catawba River along the North Carolina–South Carolina line, bordered by Gaston and Mecklenburg counties in North Carolina and York County in South Carolina. According to the SC Department of Natural Resources (<https://dnr.sc.gov/lakes/wylie/description.html>) , the lake covers about 13,400 acres with roughly 325 miles of shoreline, and it's owned and managed by Duke Energy.

A waterfront purchase has more moving parts than a typical home sale. You're buying a house, a shoreline and often a dock, each with its own rules and risks. This guide focuses on the South Carolina side of the lake. For lifestyle and neighborhood information, see our Lake Wylie homebuyer guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/living-lake-wylie-sc-complete-2026-homebuyer-guide/>) .

## What kind of water access are you buying?

| Type | What you get | What to check

| Direct lakefront | Your lot meets the shoreline; you may have or add a private dock | Survey, Duke Energy dock permit, depth, shoreline condition

| Deeded access | A recorded right to reach the water by path, easement or shared launch | The exact wording in the deed and any shared-maintenance terms

| Community amenities | Shared docks, slips, swim areas or a clubhouse | HOA rules, slip availability and waiting lists, dues

| Water view | A view of the lake, no private access | Whether the view could be blocked; don't pay a waterfront premium

Listings use "lake home" loosely. Read the deed and plat, not just the listing description.

## How do you judge the shoreline and depth?

Two homes of the same size can differ a lot in value because of the shoreline:

- Depth at the dock: if you'll keep a boat, ask what the depth is when the lake is lower than full pond. Duke Energy publishes current levels and explains how they're managed on its lake level basics (<https://www.duke-energy.com/community/lakes/dam-and-lake-level-basics>) page.

- Shoreline type: rocky or stabilized banks are usually more stable. Soft banks can erode and may need riprap or other stabilization, which requires permitting.

- Cove or open water: coves are calmer for swimming and paddling. Open water has bigger views but more wave action on docks.

- Usable frontage: a wide, gentle slope to the water is worth more than a narrow strip at the tip of a lot. Walk the whole waterfront.

## What does Duke Energy control?

Duke Energy operates the Wylie Hydroelectric Station and manages lake levels. It also reviews docks, boat lifts and most shoreline changes through its shoreline permitting program (<https://www.duke-energy.com/community/lakes/services/permits-shoreline-activities>) , in addition to any York County or Gaston County building permits.

Before you commit, confirm:

- Is the existing dock permitted, and does its current size and layout match the permit?

- Are there any open violations or unresolved permit issues?

- If you plan to add or expand a dock, what will the rules allow on this lot?

Unpermitted additions can become your problem after closing.

## How should you inspect the dock?

Hire a dock or marine inspector in addition to your home inspector. Ask them to check:

- Decking and framing: composite decking lasts longer; older treated wood needs more upkeep.

- Pilings and floats: look for rot, damage or movement at the waterline.

- Electrical: dock power for lights, lifts and shore power needs to meet code for wet locations. Ask for inspection records.

- Boat lift: condition, capacity and motor operation.

## What will insurance cost?

Standard homeowners policies don't cover flood damage. Look up the property on FEMA's Flood Map Service Center (<https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home>) . If it's in a Special Flood Hazard Area and you have a federally backed mortgage, flood insurance is required. Even outside those zones, many lakefront owners carry it.

- Get quotes through the National Flood Insurance Program (<https://www.floodsmart.gov/>) and from private flood insurers.

- Ask the seller for their current flood policy and any elevation certificate.

- Expect homeowners premiums for waterfront homes to differ from inland homes, and get quotes before your due diligence period ends.

## How are property taxes different in South Carolina?

South Carolina assesses an owner-occupied legal residence at 4% of its value, compared with 6% for second homes and rentals. You have to apply with the county to get the 4% rate. If the lake home will be your primary residence, ask the York County assessor's office about the application, and confirm the current tax bill on any property you're considering. The SC Department of Revenue (<https://dor.sc.gov/>) explains property tax basics.

On the North Carolina side, homes are taxed at assessed value set by each county's revaluation. Compare the actual tax bills on homes you're weighing on each side of the lake.

## Does the lake change through the year?

- Summer: peak boating season. Weekend traffic picks up, especially on open water.

- Fall and winter: quieter, and levels may run lower, which can affect shallow docks.

- Spring: activity picks back up as the weather warms.

If you're buying a second home, think honestly about how many weekends you'll use it.

## How does financing work for waterfront homes?

- Appraisals: waterfront comparables are limited, so appraisals can be harder. Ask whether your lender uses appraisers familiar with lake properties.

- Jumbo loans: many lakefront homes are priced above conforming loan limits. Requirements for down payment, credit and reserves vary by lender.

- Second homes: terms differ from a primary residence. Tell your lender up front how you'll use the home.

- Insurance and qualifying: required flood insurance is part of your monthly payment and affects your debt-to-income ratio.

Our preferred lender (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/our-preferred-lender/>) page and mortgage calculator (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mortgage-calculator/>) can help you plan.

## Waterfront buyer checklist

- Confirm the access type in the deed and plat.

- Verify the dock's Duke Energy permit and compare it to what's built.

- Ask about depth at the dock in lower-water months.

- Order a home inspection and a separate dock inspection.

- Check the FEMA flood zone and get flood and homeowners quotes.

- Review HOA documents for dock, slip and shoreline rules.

- Confirm property taxes and your eligibility for the 4% rate.

- Line up financing that fits waterfront and, if needed, jumbo loans.

Ready to tour? Talk With a Buyer's Agent, and we'll start with the parts of the lake that fit your plans. More on the area is on our Lake Wylie community page (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/lake-wylie/>) .

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I swim and boat from any Lake Wylie waterfront home?

Generally yes, but what you can build or keep at the shoreline depends on Duke Energy rules, depth and any HOA restrictions. Check those before you buy.

### Who patrols and regulates boating on Lake Wylie?

Law enforcement from Gaston, Mecklenburg and York counties all patrol the lake, and the Lake Wylie Marine Commission works on safety and lake issues across the jurisdictions.

### Is a water-access home a good compromise?

It can be. Deeded access or community docks cost less than direct frontage, but read exactly what rights come with the home, and check slip availability before you count on one.

### What extra costs come with a lakefront home?

Budget for flood insurance, possibly higher homeowners premiums, dock and lift maintenance, shoreline stabilization if needed, permit fees for dock changes, and HOA dues if the home is in a managed community.

Title: What to Look for During Home Tours in Charlotte, NC
Summary: A practical, room-by-room checklist for Charlotte home tours, from the roofline and crawlspace to the questions your agent should ask.

Buying (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/buying/>) Charlotte, NCNo. 113

# What to Look for During Home Tours in Charlotte, NC

A practical, room-by-room checklist for Charlotte home tours, from the roofline and crawlspace to the questions your agent should ask.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 17, 20264 min read

In this article

- What should you check outside before going in?
- How do you evaluate the neighborhood?
- What should you check room by room?
- Which major systems should you ask about?
- How do you spot water damage?
- What does a home's age tell you?
- What questions should your agent ask?
- How do you keep tours straight?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

On a Charlotte home tour, look past staging to the bones: roof, gutters, grading and foundation outside; water stains, soft tile and musty smells inside; and the age of the HVAC, water heater, electrical panel and plumbing. Check the neighborhood, school assignment and road noise too, take notes, and confirm everything with a professional inspection.

## Key takeaways

- Start outside: roof, gutters, grading and foundation cracks tell you a lot before you open the door.
- Moisture is a common, costly problem in the Piedmont's clay soils and summer storms; look and smell for it.
- Ask the age of every major system: HVAC, water heater, roof, electrical panel and plumbing type.
- A home's era hints at likely issues, from lead paint before 1978 to polybutylene pipe and synthetic stucco later.
- Confirm school assignment with Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools and always follow up with an inspection.

Listing photos are taken to show every room at its best. A tour is your chance to notice what photos can't: a musty crawlspace, traffic noise from a nearby interchange, floors that dip or rooms that never get sun. Charlotte's housing stock runs from 1920s bungalows in Dilworth to new construction in Ballantyne and beyond, so each tour can surface different issues. Use this checklist to make every walkthrough count.

## What should you check outside before going in?

Spend a few minutes walking the exterior. Charlotte's hot summers, heavy storms and occasional ice can expose weak spots.

- Roof: Missing, curling or discolored shingles. Ask when it was last replaced.
- Gutters and downspouts: Clogged or poorly pitched gutters send water toward the house.
- Grading: The ground should slope away from the foundation.
- Foundation and brick: Hairline cracks are common. Wide, horizontal or stair-step cracks deserve a closer look.
- Driveway and walks: Heaving or badly cracked concrete can point to soil movement or drainage problems.

The Piedmont's red clay soils hold water and can move with the seasons, which is why drainage and foundation condition matter throughout the region.

## How do you evaluate the neighborhood?

- Roads and noise: Homes near I-77, I-85, I-485 or busy connectors can have noise you won't notice from the listing.
- Schools: Confirm assignment with the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools (<https://www.cms.k12.nc.us/>) address lookup; boundaries don't always follow neighborhood lines.
- Walkability: Areas like Dilworth, Plaza Midwood, NoDa and South End offer walkable restaurants and greenways. More suburban areas usually mean larger lots and more driving.
- Future development: Check for planned road projects or rezoning nearby.
- HOA: Ask about dues, rules and any pending special assessments.

See our Charlotte community guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/charlotte/>) for more neighborhood context.

## What should you check room by room?

| Room | What to check

| Kitchen | Open cabinets and drawers, look under the sink for stains or soft wood, test included appliances, look for gaps in counters or backsplash

| Bathrooms | Press on tile around tubs and showers for give, check caulk around tub and toilet base, run faucets and flush toilets, confirm the exhaust fan works

| Bedrooms | Closet size, window condition (rotting frames, foggy glass), ceiling fans, outlet placement

| Living areas | Soft spots or uneven floors, condition of hardwoods, fireplace and chimney

| Basement or crawlspace | Musty smell, standing water, white mineral deposits on walls, vapor barrier

| Attic (if accessible) | Insulation level, signs of leaks, ventilation

## Which major systems should you ask about?

- HVAC: Ask its age and service history. Listen when it cycles on and feel for airflow in every room. In a Charlotte summer, this system matters.
- Plumbing: Check water pressure and drains. Ask whether pipes are copper, PEX, galvanized or polybutylene; older galvanized and polybutylene pipe can be a concern.
- Electrical: Note the panel brand and capacity. Older homes may have smaller panels or aluminum branch wiring that an electrician should evaluate. Kitchens and baths should have GFCI outlets.
- Water heater: The manufacture date is usually on the label. Note tank or tankless.

## How do you spot water damage?

Water intrusion is one of the most expensive problems buyers run into. Look and smell for:

- Ceiling stains, especially under bathrooms or near the roofline
- Musty odors in basements, crawlspaces, closets or utility rooms
- Warped baseboards or buckled flooring
- Discoloration around window frames
- Mold in grout, under sinks or in closets

Signs of moisture aren't always a reason to walk away. They're a reason to make sure your due diligence period covers a thorough inspection and, if needed, a specialist.

## What does a home's age tell you?

- Built before 1978: Possible lead-based paint (sellers must provide the federal lead disclosure; see the EPA's guidance (<https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure>) ) and possible asbestos-containing materials. Often great character and original hardwoods.
- 1970s through 1990s: Watch for polybutylene plumbing, aluminum branch wiring in some homes and synthetic stucco (EIFS) that can trap moisture.
- New construction: Fewer maintenance issues, but research the builder, read the warranty and still get an independent inspection.

Ally also runs Bohanan Construction (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/bohanan-construction/>) , which builds custom homes in Gastonia, so she tours with a builder's eye for how a house is put together.

## What questions should your agent ask?

- How long has it been on the market, and has the price changed?
- Why are the sellers moving, and what timing do they want?
- Are there known issues, past repairs or insurance claims?
- What conveys: appliances, fixtures, window treatments?
- Are there HOA violations or pending assessments?
- What are average utility costs?

Your agent can turn those answers into offer strategy. Learn more about buyer agent services (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/buyer-agent-services-in-gastonia-nc/>) .

## How do you keep tours straight?

After a few homes, everything blurs. Take photos of anything that concerns you and jot notes right after each tour: system ages, condition of windows and doors, visible repairs, parking and your gut feeling about the street.

Tip: Visit your top choice a second time at a different time of day. Traffic, noise and natural light can feel completely different at 8 a.m. and 6 p.m.

A home that feels right matters, but let the inspection confirm it. When you're ready to tour, Talk With a Buyer's Agent using the form below.

Sources cited in this article: cms.k12.nc.us (<https://www.cms.k12.nc.us/>) , epa.gov (<https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure>) . Figures are as reported by those sources at the time of writing.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many homes should I tour before making an offer?

There's no set number. Many buyers tour enough homes to understand what their budget buys in their target areas, then move quickly when the right one appears.

### Should I get an inspection on a new-construction home in Charlotte?

Yes. An independent inspector can catch installation issues before closing, and some buyers also schedule an inspection before the builder's one-year warranty ends.

### What should I bring to a home tour?

Bring your list of must-haves, a phone for photos and notes, and a small flashlight for closets and under sinks. Wear shoes that are easy to slip off.

### How long should a home tour take?

For a home you're seriously considering, plan on at least 30 minutes so you can walk the exterior, open cabinets and check systems without rushing.

Title: Appraisal Tips to Avoid Last-Minute Surprises in Lowell, NC
Summary: How appraisals work in a small Gaston County town, what to prepare before the appraiser arrives, and what to do if the number comes in low.

Selling (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/selling/>) Lowell, NCNo. 112

# Appraisal Tips to Avoid Last-Minute Surprises in Lowell, NC

How appraisals work in a small Gaston County town, what to prepare before the appraiser arrives, and what to do if the number comes in low.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 16, 2026Updated November 16, 20264 min read

In this article

- What does an appraiser actually look at?
- Why are comps tricky in Lowell?
- What should sellers fix before the appraisal?
- How do you make sure your upgrades are counted?
- What does appraisal day look like?
- How should buyers plan for the appraisal?
- What if the appraisal comes in low?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

To avoid appraisal surprises in Lowell, price your home from truly comparable recent sales, fix visible safety and maintenance issues early, and give the appraiser a written list of upgrades with dates. Buyers should know their plan for an appraisal gap before signing, and try to get the appraisal back within the due diligence period.

## Key takeaways

- Lowell's mix of older homes and newer construction means good comps can be scarce, so pricing has to start from carefully chosen sales.
- Appraisers note visible defects like roof wear, leaks and peeling paint, and some loans require repairs before closing.
- A one-page upgrade list with dates, permits and warranties helps the appraiser credit your improvements.
- Buyers should decide in advance how much of an appraisal gap they can cover in cash.
- A low appraisal can be challenged with better comps through the lender's reconsideration process, or renegotiated.

Appraisals cause more last-minute stress than almost any other part of a sale. The buyer and seller have agreed on a price, the inspection is done, and then a number comes back that doesn't match. In a small town like Lowell, where homes range from older mill-era houses to newer construction, that risk is real. The good news is that most appraisal problems can be seen coming. Here's how to prepare.

## What does an appraiser actually look at?

When a buyer uses a mortgage, the lender orders an independent appraisal to confirm the home is worth the loan. The appraiser looks at:

- Comparable sales: recent closed sales of similar homes nearby.

- The home itself: square footage, bedrooms and baths, lot, layout and quality of construction.

- Condition: visible wear, maintenance and anything that affects safety or livability.

- Location: the street, the neighborhood and features like a busy road or a wooded lot.

Appraisers aren't judging your decor. They are judging whether the market supports the price.

## Why are comps tricky in Lowell?

Lowell is a small town between Gastonia and McAdenville, just off I-85. There simply aren't as many sales here as in Gastonia or Belmont, and the housing stock is mixed. That means:

- The appraiser may need to use sales from a wider area, including nearby Gastonia, Cramerton or McAdenville.

- Comps may be older than usual, which requires adjustments for market changes.

- Two homes with similar square footage can differ a lot in value because of updates, layout or lot.

This is why pricing from online estimates is risky. If the list price is built on homes that aren't really comparable, the appraisal is where it falls apart. Our guide to reading comps in Lowell (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-read-comps-like-a-pro-in-lowell-nc/>) explains how to judge a comp the way an appraiser would.

## What should sellers fix before the appraisal?

Focus on safety, function and obvious maintenance. Cosmetic projects rarely move an appraisal; deferred maintenance can lower the condition rating and, with some loans, create repair requirements that delay closing.

| Fix first | Usually optional

| Roof leaks, missing shingles, water stains | Trend-driven paint colors

| Peeling paint, especially on older homes | New light fixtures in working condition

| Non-working HVAC, plumbing leaks | Minor landscaping upgrades

| Exposed wiring, missing outlet covers, broken handrails | Replacing dated but functional cabinets

| Rotted wood, foundation cracks, drainage problems | Decorative updates

FHA and VA appraisals in particular can call out safety and condition items that must be addressed before the loan closes. Handling them before you list is usually faster and cheaper than handling them under a deadline.

## How do you make sure your upgrades are counted?

Appraisers rely on evidence. If they don't know the roof is three years old or the bathrooms were redone with permits, they can't credit it. Prepare a one-page upgrade list with:

- What was done (roof, HVAC, windows, kitchen, flooring, additions).

- When it was done.

- Permits for major work, if any.

- Warranties that transfer to the buyer.

- Before-and-after photos for big projects.

Upgrades don't add value dollar for dollar, but documented, permitted work supports better condition and quality adjustments. This is especially true for custom or high-end homes where features aren't obvious from a walk-through.

## What does appraisal day look like?

- Make sure all utilities are on.

- Clear access to the attic, crawl space, garage, electrical panel and any outbuildings.

- Replace burned-out bulbs and secure pets.

- Leave your upgrade list on the kitchen counter.

- Tidy up. Clutter won't change the value, but a clean home signals good maintenance.

Your agent can share relevant comps and the upgrade list, but federal appraiser independence rules mean no one can pressure the appraiser toward a number.

## How should buyers plan for the appraisal?

If you're buying in Lowell, think about the appraisal before you write your offer, not after.

- Know your gap budget. If you offer above recent sales, decide how much cash you could add if the appraisal comes in short.

- Watch your due diligence timeline. In North Carolina's standard contract, much of a buyer's protection comes from the due diligence period. Ask your lender to order the appraisal early so you have the result before that period ends.

- Understand your loan. Lenders base the loan on the lower of the price or the appraised value, so a low appraisal means more cash or a renegotiation.

Our buyer agent services (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/buyer-agent-services-in-gastonia-nc/>) page covers how we structure offers around these risks.

## What if the appraisal comes in low?

You have options:

- Review the report. Check for errors in square footage, bedroom count or features.

- Request a reconsideration of value. Through the lender, submit better comparable sales the appraiser may have missed. Lenders have formal processes for this.

- Renegotiate. The seller lowers the price, the buyer covers the gap, or both meet in the middle.

- Change the loan. Sometimes a different down payment or loan structure helps.

- Walk away if your contract allows. Timing and contract terms matter here, so talk to your agent before deadlines pass.

Tip for sellers: A realistic list price is the best appraisal insurance there is. Pricing from carefully chosen comps protects you from a renegotiation two weeks before closing.

Learn more about selling in the area on our Lowell community page (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/lowell/>) and selling guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/sell-your-home-in-gastonia-nc/>) . If you're getting ready to list, Request a Pricing Consultation and we'll walk through your comps together.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I be at the appraisal for my Lowell home?

Yes, sellers can usually be present, but keep it brief. Let the appraiser in, hand over your upgrade list and access instructions, and give them room to work.

### How is an appraisal different from a home inspection?

An appraisal estimates market value for the lender, while an inspection looks at condition in detail for the buyer. Appraisers note obvious condition issues but don't test systems the way an inspector does.

### Will an online estimate match my appraisal?

Not necessarily. Automated estimates can't see your home's condition, updates or the specific street it's on, and in a small town with few recent sales they can be well off.

### What happens if the appraisal comes in higher than the price?

Nothing changes in the deal; the buyer simply starts with some built-in equity. The loan is based on the lower of the price or the appraised value.

Title: Best Neighborhoods for Homebuyers in Belmont, NC
Summary: Downtown, McLean, Reflection Pointe, Catawba Heights and Belmont's new construction compared, so you can match a neighborhood to how you want to live.

Communities (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/communities/>) Belmont, NCNo. 111

# Best Neighborhoods for Homebuyers in Belmont, NC

Downtown, McLean, Reflection Pointe, Catawba Heights and Belmont's new construction compared, so you can match a neighborhood to how you want to live.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 15, 20264 min read

In this article

- How do Belmont's neighborhoods compare?
- Why do so many buyers choose Belmont?
- Is downtown Belmont right for you?
- What does McLean offer?
- What does Reflection Pointe offer?
- Where can you get more house for the money?
- Should you buy new construction in Belmont?
- How do you choose the right Belmont neighborhood?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

The best Belmont neighborhood depends on your priorities. Downtown Belmont suits buyers who want to walk to restaurants and Stowe Park. McLean and Reflection Pointe offer Lake Wylie access and amenities. Catawba Heights and older areas often offer more house for the money, and new-construction communities suit buyers who want modern plans and warranties.

## Key takeaways

- Downtown Belmont is the choice for walkability: three historic districts, Main Street shops and Stowe Park.
- McLean and Reflection Pointe are amenity-rich Lake Wylie communities, and both carry HOA dues worth reviewing.
- Older, established areas tend to offer more space and value but may need updates.
- In new construction, the builder's sales agent represents the builder, so bring your own buyer's agent.
- Confirm school assignments with Gaston County Schools for each specific address.

Belmont sits on the Catawba River just across from Charlotte, and it has become one of the most sought-after towns in Gaston County. It has a walkable downtown, real community events and a range of neighborhoods, from historic bungalows to gated lake communities. Ally's office is on North Main Street, so this is home turf.

Here's how Belmont's main neighborhood types compare. Prices change, so ask us for recent sales in any area you're considering.

## How do Belmont's neighborhoods compare?

| Neighborhood | Best for | Home types | Things to check

| Downtown and the historic districts | Walkability, character | Historic bungalows, cottages, newer infill | Age of systems, lot size, historic-district rules

| McLean | Lake Wylie access, trails, newer homes | Townhomes to custom single-family | HOA dues and section-by-section amenities

| Reflection Pointe | Gated lake living, amenities | Custom and semi-custom homes, lots | HOA dues, boat slip and storage rules

| Catawba Heights and established areas | Value and space | Ranches, bungalows, some newer homes | Updates needed, drainage, flood zones near the river

| New-construction communities | Modern plans, warranties | Townhomes to single-family | Builder contract, upgrade costs, completion dates

## Why do so many buyers choose Belmont?

- A real downtown. Three historic districts, Main Street shops, coffee houses and Belmont Bookshop, plus Stowe Park for farmers markets, concerts and the December Festival of Trees.

- Water and outdoors. Kevin Loftin Riverfront Park on the Catawba, the sandy Lake Wylie shoreline at South Point Access and the Rocky Branch Park mountain-bike trails.

- Daniel Stowe Conservancy. The botanical garden south of downtown lights up for Holidays at the Garden each December.

- Location. Belmont is a short drive to uptown Charlotte and Charlotte Douglas International Airport, while still feeling like a small town.

Property taxes are a common question. Gaston County and Mecklenburg County rates change with revaluations, so compare the current rates on the Gaston County tax office (<https://www.gastongov.com/583/Tax-Office>) site with Mecklenburg's before you assume one is cheaper.

For more on day-to-day life, see our Belmont community page (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/belmont/>) .

## Is downtown Belmont right for you?

If you want to walk out your front door to dinner, coffee or a festival, downtown is the clear choice. You'll find historic bungalows and Craftsman-style homes alongside newer infill, ranging from small cottages to fully renovated family homes.

The trade-offs are typical of older homes: smaller lots, older plumbing, wiring and HVAC, and sometimes less storage. A thorough inspection and a look at the home's update history matter here. Our guide to buying near downtown Belmont (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/buying-near-downtown-belmont-pros-and-cons/>) covers the pros and cons in more depth.

## What does McLean offer?

McLean is a master-planned community on Belmont's south side, along about five miles of Lake Wylie shoreline, according to the McLean community site (<https://discovermclean.com/>) . It has more than ten miles of trails, connects to the Carolina Thread Trail's Seven Oaks Preserve and sits next to Daniel Stowe Conservancy. A marina serves the community.

Homes range from townhomes to larger custom builds, and amenities vary by section. Because demand is strong, have your pre-approval ready before you tour.

## What does Reflection Pointe offer?

Reflection Pointe is a gated community on Lake Wylie with resort-style amenities: a clubhouse, pool, tennis courts, walking trails, a community beach and a marina area with boat storage. Homes include larger custom builds, and the community also has lots for buyers who want to build.

Before you buy, ask the HOA about dues, what they include, rules on boat slips and storage, and architectural guidelines if you plan to build.

## Where can you get more house for the money?

Catawba Heights and other established areas on the edges of Belmont, including toward Cramerton, tend to offer a mix of mid-century ranches, updated bungalows and some newer homes. Many have larger lots and fewer HOA rules than master-planned communities.

These areas are often a good fit for first-time buyers and anyone who wants space without lake-community dues. Expect some homes to need updates, and check flood maps for properties near the river. Our mortgage calculator (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/mortgage-calculator/>) can help you compare monthly payments as you narrow your list.

## Should you buy new construction in Belmont?

Belmont has seen steady new-construction activity, from townhomes to single-family homes. New homes offer modern floor plans, energy efficiency and builder warranties, and you may get to choose finishes.

One important point: the builder's on-site sales agent represents the builder, not you. Your own buyer's agent can review the purchase agreement, compare upgrade pricing and keep an eye on inspections and the punch list. See our guide to new construction homes in Belmont (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/new-construction-homes-in-belmont-nc/>) .

If you'd rather build a fully custom home, Ally also runs Bohanan Construction (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/bohanan-construction/>) , a Gastonia custom home builder.

## How do you choose the right Belmont neighborhood?

- Test your commute. Drive it at rush hour from each neighborhood you're considering.

- Confirm school assignments. Belmont is served by Gaston County Schools, and assignments are by address. Check each property with the district before you write an offer.

- Read the HOA documents. Know the dues, what they cover, the reserves and the rules.

- Think about long-term value. Proximity to downtown, the lake and planned development all affect demand.

- Match the neighborhood to your lifestyle. A lake community is ideal if you'll use the water; downtown is better if you want to walk everywhere.

Before you tour, talk with our preferred lender (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/our-preferred-lender/>) about pre-approval so you know your comfortable price range. When you're ready to compare neighborhoods in person, Talk With a Buyer's Agent and we'll plan the route.

## Frequently asked questions

### Which Belmont neighborhood is best for commuting to Charlotte?

Neighborhoods closer to downtown Belmont and the I-85 interchanges usually have the quickest drive into Charlotte. Lake communities on the South Point peninsula are farther from the interstate, so test-drive your commute at rush hour before you decide.

### Do Belmont lake communities have HOA fees?

Yes. Amenity-rich communities such as McLean and Reflection Pointe have HOA dues that fund pools, clubhouses, trails and marina areas. Ask for the current dues, what they cover, any special assessments and the rules on boats, docks and rentals.

### Is Belmont a good place for first-time buyers?

It can be, especially in older, established neighborhoods and townhome communities. Check whether you qualify for programs through the NC Housing Finance Agency and get pre-approved before you tour, since well-priced Belmont homes can move quickly.

### Can I build a custom home in Belmont?

Yes. Several Belmont communities, including Reflection Pointe, sell lots for custom homes, and you'll also find infill lots in older areas. Check HOA architectural rules and utilities before you buy the lot.

Title: What to Look for in Disclosures in Cherryville, NC
Summary: How to read North Carolina seller disclosures on a Cherryville home, what "No Representation" means, and which answers deserve follow-up.

Buying (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/buying/>) Cherryville, NCNo. 110

# What to Look for in Disclosures in Cherryville, NC

How to read North Carolina seller disclosures on a Cherryville home, what "No Representation" means, and which answers deserve follow-up.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 13, 2026Updated November 16, 20263 min read

In this article

- What disclosure forms will you see in North Carolina?
- What does "No Representation" mean?
- What does the form cover?
- Which Cherryville issues deserve extra attention?
- What are the red flags?
- How should you follow up?
- What should Cherryville sellers know?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

When buying in Cherryville, read the North Carolina Residential Property and Owners' Association Disclosure Statement and the mineral and oil and gas rights disclosure before you offer. Look closely at water, wells, septic, roof, foundation, systems, zoning and access answers. Treat "No Representation" as no information, not a clean bill of health, and verify everything with inspections and records.

## Key takeaways

- North Carolina law lets sellers disclose what they actually know, or choose "No Representation."
- "No Representation" means the seller isn't making statements, not that nothing is wrong.
- Rural Cherryville properties often need extra attention to wells, septic, drainage and access.
- Patterns of repeated repairs and missing permits are the red flags to chase down.
- Disclosures are a starting point; your inspections and due diligence do the real verifying.

Cherryville, in western Gaston County, has a mix of older in-town homes, newer houses and rural properties with acreage. Each comes with its own disclosure issues. Here's how North Carolina disclosures work and what to look for when you review them on a Cherryville home.

## What disclosure forms will you see in North Carolina?

Under the Residential Property Disclosure Act (Chapter 47E) (<https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/ByChapter/Chapter_47E.html>) , most sellers of one- to four-unit homes must give buyers:

- The Residential Property and Owners' Association Disclosure Statement, a standard form developed by the North Carolina Real Estate Commission (<https://www.ncrec.gov/>)
- The Mineral and Oil and Gas Rights Mandatory Disclosure Statement

The law says sellers should deliver these no later than when you make your offer. If you don't receive them before you offer, you may have a short window to cancel the contract, which expires at the earliest of three calendar days after you receive them, three calendar days after the contract is made, or closing or occupancy. Some transfers are exempt, including estate sales by a fiduciary and foreclosures, and first sales of never-occupied new homes are exempt from the residential form but not the mineral rights form.

## What does "No Representation" mean?

For each question, North Carolina sellers can answer based on what they actually know or choose "No Representation." That choice is legal. It means the seller isn't making a statement about that item, not that the item is fine. Many sellers who haven't lived in a home, like heirs or investors, choose it for most questions.

Sellers still can't actively hide or misrepresent problems, and real estate brokers must disclose material facts they know or reasonably should know. But you shouldn't rely on the form alone. Treat any "No Representation" answer on a major item as a prompt to inspect it.

## What does the form cover?

| Topic | What to look for

| Water and sewer | Public vs private well; septic type and any known problems

| Structure | Roof, chimneys, floors, foundation, basement or crawlspace, and any modifications

| Systems | Plumbing, electrical, heating, cooling and other mechanical systems

| Wood-destroying insects | Current infestation or unrepaired past damage

| Land use | Zoning, restrictive covenants, encroachments and government notices

| Environmental | Lead-based paint, asbestos, radon, underground storage tanks and other contamination

| Owners' association | Dues, assessments, covenants and who maintains common areas

Homes built before 1978 also require a federal lead-based paint disclosure (<https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure>) .

## Which Cherryville issues deserve extra attention?

### Water and drainage

Larger parcels can have creeks, low areas or natural drainage paths, and heavy rain can cause problems even away from mapped floodplains. Check the FEMA flood map (<https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search>) , look for standing water or crawlspace moisture, and ask about past water intrusion.

### Wells and septic

Many rural Cherryville properties rely on a private well and septic system. Ask for septic permits and pumping records, and plan a septic inspection and water test during your due diligence period. Gaston County environmental health may have records.

### Older homes

Older in-town homes may have original wiring, older plumbing materials or renovations done before current permitting standards. Ask for permits on additions and finished spaces.

### Access and land use

Rural parcels may share driveways or private roads. Ask whether there's a recorded maintenance agreement. Check zoning and any restrictions if you plan to add outbuildings, keep animals or subdivide. Look into nearby agricultural or other land uses too.

## What are the red flags?

- Several repairs to the same system over a short time
- Water intrusion or mold mentioned without details on how it was fixed
- "No Representation" on major systems from a seller who has lived in the home for years
- Additions, garage conversions or finished basements without permits
- A recent renovation or flip with no contractor information or warranties
- Recent insurance claims for storm, fire or water damage
- Answers that conflict with what you see at the showing

## How should you follow up?

- Read the disclosures before you offer and write down questions.
- Ask your agent to request receipts, permits, warranties and service records.
- Book a general home inspection early in your due diligence period, plus specialists where needed: septic, well water, structural, roof, HVAC, radon or wood-destroying insects.
- Check permits with the city or county for major work.
- Use what you find to negotiate repairs or credits, or to terminate before your due diligence period ends.

## What should Cherryville sellers know?

Complete the form carefully and honestly. Gather records before listing, and consider fixing known issues or pricing accordingly. Clear, documented answers build buyer confidence and reduce surprises during due diligence. If you're preparing to sell, see how to declutter before listing in Cherryville (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-declutter-before-listing-your-home-in-cherryville-nc/>) and Request a Pricing Consultation.

Buying in Cherryville? Read our guide to buying land in Cherryville (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/how-to-buy-land-for-a-custom-home-in-cherryville-nc/>) , and Talk With a Buyer's Agent before you write an offer.

Sources cited in this article: ncleg.gov (<https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/ByChapter/Chapter_47E.html>) , NC Real Estate Commission (<https://www.ncrec.gov/>) , epa.gov (<https://www.epa.gov/lead/real-estate-disclosure>) , FEMA Flood Map Service Center (<https://msc.fema.gov/portal/search>) . Figures are as reported by those sources at the time of writing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do disclosures replace a home inspection?

No. Disclosures share what the seller knows or choose not to address. An inspection looks for conditions the seller may not know about or didn't disclose.

### Do disclosures differ for new construction?

First sales of never-occupied homes are exempt from the residential property disclosure form, though the mineral and oil and gas rights disclosure still applies. Ask the builder for warranties and inspection records.

### Should sellers fix problems before listing or disclose them?

Sellers aren't required to fix everything. Fixing key issues can improve marketability, and accurate disclosure of known issues avoids problems later.

### What if I didn't get disclosures before making an offer?

North Carolina law gives you a short window to cancel, generally ending three calendar days after you receive the forms or after the contract is made, whichever comes first, or at closing or occupancy. Talk with your agent or attorney right away.

Title: Why More Buyers Are Moving to Clover, SC | Ally Bohanan

Communities (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/blog-realtor-in-gastonia-nc/topic/communities/>) Clover, SCNo. 109

# Why More Buyers Are Moving to Clover, SC

What draws buyers to Clover in York County, the trade-offs to weigh, and what moving across the state line from North Carolina involves.

By Ally Bohanan (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/about-ally-bohanan/>) Published June 11, 20263 min read

In this article

- Where is Clover, and how connected is it?
- What draws buyers to Clover?
- What kinds of homes are available?
- What trade-offs should you weigh?
- What changes when you move from North Carolina to South Carolina?
- How should you start your Clover search?
- Frequently asked questions

The short answer

Buyers are moving to Clover, SC for a small-town setting in York County, newer homes and larger lots, the Clover School District, and nearby Lake Wylie, while staying within reach of Charlotte, Gastonia and Rock Hill. If you're coming from North Carolina, plan for South Carolina's owner-occupied 4% assessment application, new vehicle and license rules and a different school system.

## Key takeaways

- Clover sits in western York County, close to Lake Wylie and the North Carolina line.
- Buyers often come for space, newer construction and the Clover School District.
- Commute times to Charlotte vary a lot by route, so test-drive them.
- South Carolina owner-occupants must apply for the 4% legal residence assessment ratio; it isn't automatic.
- Moving from NC means new state license, registration, voter and tax steps.

Clover is a small town in western York County, South Carolina, just south of the North Carolina line and west of Lake Wylie. It has drawn steady interest from buyers in Charlotte, Gaston County and beyond. Here's what attracts them, what to weigh and what to plan for if you're moving from North Carolina.

## Where is Clover, and how connected is it?

Clover sits between Gastonia to the north, Lake Wylie to the east, Rock Hill and Fort Mill to the southeast and York to the south. SC-55 and US-321 are the main routes through the area, and many residents reach Charlotte via the Lake Wylie area or I-85 through Gaston County. Commute times depend heavily on your destination and time of day, so drive your route at rush hour before you buy.

## What draws buyers to Clover?

### More space for the budget

Many buyers find more square footage, larger yards or newer construction than they could get for the same budget closer to Charlotte. Prices vary widely by neighborhood, lot and age, so compare recent sales in the specific areas you're considering.

### Schools

Clover is served by the Clover School District (<https://www.clover.k12.sc.us/>) , which is a major reason many families look here. Assignments depend on the exact address, and growth can change attendance zones, so confirm before you buy.

### Small-town feel

Clover's downtown, local restaurants and community events give it a different pace than the larger suburbs. Visit on a weekend and a weekday evening to see how it fits you.

### Lake Wylie nearby

Boating, fishing and lake-area living are a short drive away, and some buyers look specifically for homes near the water or in lake-access communities. Read our Lake Wylie community guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/lake-wylie/>) .

## What kinds of homes are available?

| Type | What to check

| Newer subdivisions | HOA dues and rules, builder warranty, school assignment

| Established in-town homes | Age of roof and systems, renovation permits

| Rural homes and acreage | Well, septic, access, flood zones and land-use rules

| Land for building | Zoning, utilities, soil and survey

If you're thinking about building, read should I buy or build (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/should-i-buy-or-build/>) . Ally also runs Bohanan Construction (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/bohanan-construction/>) , which builds custom homes in Gastonia.

## What trade-offs should you weigh?

- Commute: longer for many Charlotte jobs, especially at peak times.
- Amenities: fewer shopping and dining options in town than in larger suburbs; many errands mean a drive to Gastonia, Rock Hill or Lake Wylie.
- Growth: new development brings options but also traffic and construction.
- Two-state life: if you work in North Carolina, ask a tax professional how working in one state and living in another affects your income taxes.

## What changes when you move from North Carolina to South Carolina?

### Property taxes

South Carolina taxes an owner-occupied primary residence at a 4% assessment ratio instead of the standard 6%, but only if you apply. York County's assessor notice (<https://www.yorkcountysc.gov/DocumentCenter/View/86/Notice-of-Assessments-PDF>) explains that owners must file an application with documentation, such as a South Carolina driver's license and vehicle registration at the property address. File promptly after closing; if you don't qualify, the 6% ratio applies.

### License, registration and voting

You'll need a South Carolina driver's license and vehicle registration, and you'll register to vote in York County. These documents also support your 4% application.

### Schools

Request records from your current school and check Clover School District enrollment requirements and dates.

### Buying in South Carolina

South Carolina uses its own contracts and disclosure forms, and closings are handled by an attorney. Your agent should be licensed in South Carolina; you can check licenses with SC LLR's Real Estate Commission (<https://www.llr.sc.gov/re/>) .

## How should you start your Clover search?

- Get pre-approved and estimate your payment, including South Carolina property tax at the 4% ratio and insurance.
- Test-drive your commute.
- Confirm school assignments for any address you're considering.
- Compare Clover with nearby York, Lake Wylie and Gastonia so you're sure it's the right fit.

Learn more on our Clover community page (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/clover/>) and in the Clover homebuyer guide (<https://allybohananrealestate.com/ally-bohanan-real-estate-preview/clover-sc-homebuyer-guide-schools-prices-commute/>) . When you're ready to tour, Talk With a Buyer's Agent.

Sources cited in this article: clover.k12.sc.us (<https://www.clover.k12.sc.us/>) , yorkcountysc.gov (<https://www.yorkcountysc.gov/DocumentCenter/View/86/Notice-of-Assessments-PDF>) , llr.sc.gov (<https://www.llr.sc.gov/re/>) . Figures are as reported by those sources at the time of writing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why are people moving to Clover, SC?

Common reasons include more space for the budget, newer homes, the Clover School District, a small-town setting and access to Lake Wylie, Gastonia and Charlotte.

### How far is Clover from Charlotte?

It's within commuting distance for many people, but drive times vary a lot by route and destination. Test your commute at rush hour.

### Do I automatically get the 4% property tax rate in South Carolina?

No. You must apply with the county assessor and show the home is your legal residence. Without approval, the 6% ratio applies.

### Can I build a custom home in Clover?

Yes, where zoning, utilities and the lot allow it. Verify those before you buy land, and involve a builder early.

Title: How Long Does It Take to Sell a Home in Clover, SC?
